new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent (realized as vowel length/quantity) distinguishes word meaning, but the author declines to give a rule for it because its placement/quantity differs from town to town; no default position is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Dialectal: the same word is pronounced 'long' in some towns and 'short' in others, which is why the author refuses to codify accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Lozano's 'lengua panayana' / 'visaya-panayana' is the 19th-century Bisayan of Panay island, i.e. the Hiligaynon (Ilonggo) area; the MPG PuRe subject tags (ceb Cebuano + hil for the 1892 item; bsd 'Bisaya, Sarawak' for the 1876 item) are cataloguing artefacts, not the content. Lozano explicitly notes town-by-town variation in accent (length) within Panay. Wolfenden 1971 (supplementary) describes the standard Iloilo Hiligaynon of the Peace Corps course.

new_statements.quote: There are twenty-six distinctive sounds in the Hiligaynon sound system, five vowels, twenty consonants, and accent. ... Accent is a combination of stress and length when it occurs with open syllables, but it is only stress elsewhere. Accent is contrasted in the following words: 'i:la they versus il'a: wild, 'a:mo master versus am'o: that is it, 'pa:nit skin versus pa'nit tuna. There is one primary accent in a word, but secondary accents (with less prominence) occur on alternate syllables from the primary accented syllable. Compare the accents on the following words: ''abu'ka:do avacado, ka''tapo'san the end, finish.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's lexical coding (Wolfenden 1971: 'twenty-five significant sounds plus accent.. Accented words have one primary stress') and with the Lozano 1876/1892 statements held by the project (accent distinguishes word meanings); adds (i) explicit minimal pairs for accent position (penult vs ultima), (ii) the phonetic make-up of accent (stress + length in open syllables, stress only elsewhere; length predictable from accent), (iii) alternating secondary accents on every other syllable from the primary, and (iv) that the practical orthography leaves accent unwritten. Minor difference of count only: 1975 says 'twenty-six distinctive sounds.. five vowels, twenty consonants, and a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent (word stress, realised as stress plus vowel length in open syllables and as stress alone in closed syllables) is a phoneme of Hiligaynon: its position is contrastive and distinguishes otherwise identical words (penult vs final: 'i:la 'they' vs il'a: 'wild', 'a:mo vs am'o:, 'pa:nit 'skin' vs pa'nit 'tuna'). Each word has exactly one primary accent; vowel length is predictable from accent (long vowels only under accent in open syllables). The practical orthography does not write accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated: 'secondary accents (with less prominence) occur on alternate syllables from the primary accented syllable', e.g. ''abu'ka:do 'avocado' (secondary on the first syllable, primary on ka:), ka''tapo'san 'the end' (secondary on ta, primary on san) - i.e. rhythmic alternating secondary accent counted from the primary.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; p. 11 notes that vowel length is predictable ('Vowels are lengthened in predictable environments. Long vowels occur only in conjunction with accent in open syllables. Compare the following words: pa:la shovel, tu:lok stare, lintaq leech'), and p. 12 that glottal stop is 'not predictable in word-final position' (segmental, not accentual). The section refers to Wolfenden (1971) for a fuller phonology.
new_statements.identity_note: Hiligaynon (Ilonggo) as spoken in Western Visayas (Iloilo/Negros Occidental; the author's SIL Philippines fieldwork and University of Hawaii 1972 dissertation, teachers named p. v include Cecile Motus); examples in the practical orthography of Hiligaynon speakers; the phonology summary is the author's own, cross-referring to his 1971 Hiligaynon Reference Grammar.

sources.quote: 'Stress is important in Hiligaynon in that it makes for a difference in meaning in some instances ... One syllable is pronounced louder than the other or others. This prominence is called stress. Example: punu' means 'tree trunk, leader, etc.' while punu' [other accent] means 'full to capacity'.' Drill lists accent pairs laba/laba', punu'/punu', bulag/bulag, pilak/pilak. (Same statement in Motus 1971 Hiligaynon Dictionary intro sec. III, fetched as : 'Stress is phonemic in Hiligaynon'.)

sources.quote: 'Word accent is very important in distinguishing forms in Hiligaynon. Roots generally have accent on either the second last or final syllable, as in: ámo 'master' (Sp.) vs. amó 'the same, thus', áyaw ... vs. ayáw ..., bála vs. balá, báti vs. batí, bílin vs. bilín, dúlot vs. dulút, súbong vs. subóng, and útud vs. utúd. If the accent falls on the second last syllable (penult) and that syllable is not closed by a consonant ... the vowel is pronounced long ...
